**The Cabinet of Useless Things**

I keep a mental cabinet of useless facts, and I'd like to show you some of the collection.

Sharks are older than trees. Sharks have been swimming for roughly 450 million years; the first true trees arrived perhaps sixty million years later. Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Apollo moon landing than to the construction of the Great Pyramid. Oxford University is older than the Aztec Empire. None of this will help you pay your taxes or fix a leaky faucet. I offer it anyway, because it sparkles.

That sparkle is a genuine puzzle. By any strict accounting, humans shouldn't care about things with no practical payoff. Survival rewards the person who knows which berry kills you, not the person who knows that octopus arms contain two-thirds of the animal's neurons and seem to taste what they touch. Yet someone, somewhere, has devoted an entire life to a single species of click beetle. When the biologist J.B.S. Haldane was asked what his studies had taught him about the mind of the Creator, he reportedly answered that God must have "an inordinate fondness for beetles" — there being some four hundred thousand known species of them. The universe, it seems, hoards variety the way I hoard facts, and someone has to admire the collection.

Consider the Antikythera mechanism. In 1901, sponge divers off a small Greek island found a first-century-BC shipwreck, and among the statues and amphorae was a corroded lump of bronze about the size of a shoebox. Decades of study revealed it to be a geared computer: turn a crank and it predicted eclipses, tracked the moon's irregular motion, and kept the calendar of the Olympic games. Nothing of comparable sophistication appears anywhere in the historical record for another thousand years. Somebody built it — some craftsman with grease on his knuckles who understood that the heavens move in ratios — and we do not know his name. His machine outlived him by two millennia and spent most of that time at the bottom of the sea.

Or consider the clouds. Until 1802, clouds had no names. Then a young London chemist and amateur meteorologist named Luke Howard delivered a lecture proposing Latin classifications, in the style of Linnaeus: cirrus, stratus, cumulus. The names caught on almost immediately, spreading across Europe like weather itself. Goethe, thrilled, wrote a series of poems in Howard's honor. Think about that. For all of human history, people had watched the sky, and no one had thought to baptize what moved through it. One man paying close attention permanently changed the vocabulary of the heavens.

Or Eratosthenes, chief librarian at Alexandria around 240 BC. He had heard that in the southern town of Syene, the noon sun on the summer solstice shone straight down a well, casting no shadow. In Alexandria, the same noon cast a shadow of about seven degrees. He measured the angle, hired someone to pace out the distance between the two cities, and computed the circumference of the entire Earth — arriving within a few percent of the true figure. The complete instrument list: a stick, a shadow, a well, and a man willing to walk. His contemporaries nicknamed him Beta, because he was reputedly second-best at everything. Second-best, and he measured the planet without leaving Egypt.

Even the people doing the preserving were delightfully human about it. Medieval monks copying manuscripts by candlelight left notes in the margins — complaints about the cold, about bad pens, about thin parchment. "Thank God, it will soon be dark," one scribe wrote at the end of a long day. Others drew knights doing battle with giant snails, for reasons no scholar has ever settled. These men were saving the entire inheritance of the ancient world one frozen page at a time, and they were also bored, and cold, and funny. Both things are in the margins.

So what is all of this for?

Honest answer: maybe nothing. And I've come to think that's precisely its dignity. We divide knowledge into the useful and the ornamental, and we defend the useful as the serious kind. But useful knowledge is, in a quiet way, always about us — our appetites, our projects, our deadlines. Useless knowledge is about the world. It is attention without an invoice, interest with no hope of repayment. Nobody studies a click beetle for forty years because it advances their career. They do it because the beetle is there, and it is strange, and strangeness deserves a witness.

There's a clue buried in the word itself. *Curiosity* descends from the Latin *curiosus*, careful, attentive — from *cura*, care. The same root gives us *cure* and *curator*. A curator is someone who cares for a collection. To be curious, then, is to extend care outward past the borders of the self, toward things that will never care back. The shark does not care that it predates the tree. The mechanism does not care that its maker's name dissolved in the sea. The clouds went unnamed for a hundred thousand years and never once complained. We care on their behalf. Somebody has to hold the other end of the thread.

The world did not have to be interesting. It could have been a gray, runny sort of place — functional, sufficient, dull. Instead it is stuffed with an almost suspicious generosity: computers in shipwrecks, poems about clouds, the circumference of a planet hiding in the shadow of a stick. Curiosity is the thank-you note we send back. It's the only one that fits in the envelope.

The puzzle of useless knowledge. By any reasonable accounting, humans shouldn't care about things with no survival payoff. Yet someone has devoted their entire life to studying a single species of click beetle. When asked what his studies of creation had taught him about the mind of God, the biologist J.B.S. Haldane reportedly answered that the Creator must have "an inordinate fondness for beetles"—there being some 400,000 known species of them.

The Antikythera mechanism: In 1901 sponge divers off a Greek island found a shipwreck from the first century BC. Among the statues and amphorae was a corroded lump of bronze. Decades of study revealed it to be a geared computer: turn a crank and it predicted eclipses, tracked the moon's irregular motion, modeled the calendar of athletic games. Nothing comparable appears in the historical record for another thousand years. Somebody built it—some craftsman with grease on his knuckles who understood that the heavens moved in ratios—and we don't know his name.

Clouds: until 1802, clouds had no names. Then a young London chemist, Luke Howard, gave a lecture proposing Linnaean-style names: cirrus, stratus, cumulus. The names caught on. Goethe, thrilled, wrote a series of poems in Howard's honor. Consider: for all of human history people had watched clouds, and no one had thought to baptize them. One man paying attention changed the sky.

Eratosthenes: Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes heard that in the southern town of Syene, the sun shone straight down a well at noon on the solstice—no shadow. In Alexandria the same noon cast a shadow. He measured the angle, hired someone to pace the distance between the cities, and computed the circumference of the Earth. He was off by only a few percent. A stick, a shadow, a well: that's the entire instrument list. His contemporaries nicknamed him Beta, because he was second-best at everything. Second best, and he measured the planet.

Marginalia: medieval monks copying manuscripts left notes in the margins—complaints about the cold, about bad pens, about the abbot. "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One wrote. They drew knights fighting snails. They preserved, by candlelight, the whole inheritance of the ancient world, one cold page at a time.

Then the turn: what is it all for?

Maybe nothing. And I think that's the fine point of it. We divide knowledge into the useful and the ornamental, and we defend the useful as serious. But the useful stuff is, in a way, merely about us—our appetites, our projects, our deadlines. Useless knowledge is about the world. It's attention without invoice.

Etymology: curiosity comes from the Latin curiosus, careful, from cura—care. The same root gives us cure and curator.
